questions.question: Justify the claim that mining is the foundation of the modern South African economy, while acknowledging its current size.
questions.expected_answer: Mining today contributes under ten per cent of GDP and employs under half a million workers, but it built the economy's structure: railways were extended inland to serve the mines, Eskom's power system grew to supply them, the JSE was founded to finance the goldfields, manufacturing and banking grew as suppliers, and Johannesburg itself exists because of Witwatersrand gold. Mining still anchors export earnings (platinum group metals, coal, iron ore, gold), pays royalties and taxes, and supports towns and multiplier jobs.

questions.question: Describe the location of South Africa's platinum mining and the factors favouring the industry.
questions.expected_answer: Platinum lies in the Bushveld Igneous Complex, a huge layered igneous body in the northern interior, mined along three limbs: western (Rustenburg/Brits, North West), eastern (Burgersfort/Steelpoort) and northern (Mokopane), following the Merensky Reef and UG2 layer. Favouring factors: exceptionally large high-grade reserves in predictable layers, a century of deep-mining expertise from gold, proximity to Gauteng's rail, power, water and skills, an established mining labour force, and strong global demand for autocatalysts, jewellery and hydrogen fuel cells.

questions.question: Explain how mining activity is identified on a topographic map, including how evidence should be presented in an answer.
questions.expected_answer: Look for the printed words Mine/Myn/Colliery/Quarry; pale, straight-edged mine dumps and rectangular slimes dams (shapes nature does not build); toothed/hachured excavation symbols; railway spurs or heavy roads dead-ending at building clusters in open country; converging power lines; and an adjacent grid-planned mining town. Present each piece of evidence as feature, map appearance and grid reference — reading eastings first, then northings.
